analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from using credit checks in hiring and employment decisions.
analysis.headline: A bill with 38 House sponsors to stop employers from checking job applicants' credit never got a committee vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to stop employers from pulling a job applicant's or employee's credit report when deciding whether to hire, fire, or promote them. It bans the practice even when the worker agrees to it, with narrow exceptions for jobs requiring national security or FDIC clearance, certain state and local government jobs, and executives at financial institutions. It never received a vote in the House committee it was assigned to.
analysis.who_benefits: Job seekers and current workers with damaged credit — often from unemployment, medical bills, or divorce — who today can be screened out of a job because of what is on their credit report, even when the job has nothing to do with handling money.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and applicants with poor credit

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act to prohibit any employer from using a consumer report containing credit information for employment purposes or for taking an adverse action against a worker, and the ban applies even if the worker consents.

It keeps narrow exceptions: jobs requiring national security or FDIC clearance, state or local government jobs that otherwise require a credit check, and supervisory, managerial, professional, or executive positions at financial institutions.

The prohibition is written to cover creditworthiness, credit standing, and credit capacity information specifically, so ordinary background checks for other purposes would continue under the law's existing disclosure rules.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus and background screening companies would lose the revenue they earn selling credit reports to employers for hiring decisions, and employers would lose a screening tool they currently use at no cost to themselves.

drawbacks.text: Employers and screening companies argue a credit report is a legitimate, inexpensive way to gauge reliability for jobs involving money or sensitive data, and the bill would take that tool away even where an applicant would voluntarily agree to the check.

The bill leaves in place many carve-outs — national security, FDIC clearance, some government jobs, and financial institution executives — so the workers it protects are those outside those categories, and supporters concede that a poor credit history can itself be a fair signal for some financial positions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a worker with medical debt or a spell of unemployment, a credit check can turn a past hardship into a permanent barrier to a job, and the research connection between personal credit and job performance is thin. The cost falls on credit bureaus and on employers who lose a cheap screen; the exceptions preserve the check where financial risk is genuinely direct. On balance the protection for workers outweighs the lost convenience for employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no bill or markup was ever scheduled, so it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the Equal Employment for All Act on January 19, 2011, with 21 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.
On March 23, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, which was its last action.

The bill gained 37 cosponsors over the course of the Congress, all of them Democrats, and none of that support produced a committee vote or floor action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and employment screening companies keep the market for employment credit checks, and employers keep using them at no cost. Workers with damaged credit remain subject to the same screening.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Consumer reporting and employment screening industry
against.role: Seller of the credit reports the bill would ban
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on the use of credit reports in employment screening.

sides.party_line_note: All 38 House members behind the bill — the sponsor and 37 cosponsors — were Democrats, and the Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Credit bureaus and employment screening companies
industries.note: These firms sell credit reports to employers for hiring decisions, a market the bill would shut off for most jobs. Their income depends on the practice, which can cost a worker a job because of old medical bills or unemployment.

industries.industry: Employers that run credit checks on applicants
industries.note: Employers would lose a free screening tool they use on most hires. They lose little money, but they lose information; workers gain protection from being screened out over credit history unrelated to the job.
